rv.q: But "Job" is a very provocative and genuinely disrupting 85 minutes with acute observational powers; you won't be bored for a millisecond.
It's muscle-tensing and entertaining, particularly in the play's middle stretch.
Too often, though, the play feels overloaded with ideas, themes and moral conundrums scattered in random bursts and bytes.
Job just cuts its knots open and leaves you with sleek, unsettling uncertainty.
If neatness is what you expect from John Guare's 'A Free Man of Color,' you'll be doomed to disappointment.
Most of the show, directed by George C. Wolfe, is a maddening slog. But the last 30 minutes are so brilliant that you can't dismiss the whole thing.
Eclecticism has always been essential to Mr. Guare's writing, which at its best juggles mismatched elements of culture, high and low, with daring and dizzying skill.
Finally, after 2 ½ hours of brain-blurring historical asides, strenuously costumed artifice and luxuriously overpopulated incoherence
From the shocking tableau that opens 'Job' right through to its excruciating final moments, Jane keeps us on the edge of our seats.
But, unlike its other less-successful, black-mirroresque peers, I promise Job’s final rattling, supreme reveal is worth it.
This makes for 80 minutes of intense, gripping action as a high-stakes psychotherapy session unfolds in real time.
But I don’t buy it — despite the cast’s considerable efforts.

Job thoughtfully gives voice to Generation Z's cynicism toward today's near-inescapably online world and their struggle to find something tangible there, even if it largely abandons the job in favor of shock value toward the end of its shift.
For all the effective stagecraft on display, however, Job mainly smacks of gimmickry.
But things go awry after a late-in-the-game twist that pushes the bounds of plausibility attempts (unsuccessfully) to move the play into psychological thriller territory.
...the tension of 'Job'...is diminished on a larger canvas
It dumps compelling societal concerns upon us, leaves them unexplored, and relies structurally on an uninspired starting point (i.e. confessing to a therapist) and gimmicks.

We get a full blast in the face of those costs in a twist that would be a spoiler to reveal, except to say that it is so shocking and implausible that it undermines much of what I found worthwhile about “Job” up until then.
Lobbing the bleakest imaginable themes at the audience simply to make the play’s lurid twists pay off makes this hollow play less of a job well done than a piece of work.
That goal is the play’s big ah-ha moment, and as plot twists goes, it crumbles at a moment’s reflection.
I suspect that "A Free Man of Color" was a lot more fun to write than it is to watch.
“Job” is a riveting psychological thriller that sustains the viewer’s attention for its entire 80-minute duration.
Job doesn’t quite do the job as a play, but enough drama remains in Friedman and Lemmon’s performances to satisfy most theatergoers.

While the stress of the former concern rises and falls and rises again, the sense of foreboding from the other one eventually fades away as the thoughtful depths of Friedlich’s compact, mind-bending two-hander become increasingly apparent.
While the text is often lumpy and filled with switchbacks, the superb performances of Friedman and Lemmon are the centerboard on this vessel.
This story of technology prevailing over humanity is disturbing because it’s disguised as a therapy session—one of the most vulnerable human experiences.
Both actors have created authentic and believable characters who manage to teeter on the cusp of truth without flinching or backing down.
Wright furiously tears around as the flamboyant Jacques.
Their interplay, especially given how articulate Jane can be at times, is consistently compelling and makes the play worth seeing.
JOB provides a novel, modern, and intriguing concept in a play that shows a tremendous amount of promise, yet still feels underbaked.
This shocker reveals Job as fundamentally in conflict with itself; playwright Max Wolf Friedlich tries to marry serious intentions to tin thrills, but his impulses cancel each other.
